title: Accuracy of Commonly Used Age-Predicted Maximal Heart Rate Equations
authors: Shookster D, Lindsey B, Cortes N, Martin JR
population: Adults in a general population completing treadmill graded exercise tests to volitional fatigue with RER > 1.10
findings: Age-predicted HRmax equations (Fox, Gellish, Gulati, Tanaka, Arena, Astrand, Nes, Fairbarn; the abstract refers to nine equations in total) were compared with HRmax from 99 treadmill graded exercise tests.
Significant differences from measured HRmax were found for the Gulati, Astrand, Nes and Fairbarn (male) equations (p < 0.05); Tanaka and Gellish were not among the significantly different equations.
Bland-Altman plots showed wide limits of agreement for all nine equations, i.e. poor agreement at the individual level.
Proportional bias: equations under-estimated HRmax in people with low measured HRmax and over-estimated it in people with high measured HRmax, except Fox.

The authors suggest the Fox (220 - age) equation may be the best option for a general population because it is less likely to under- or over-estimate by individual HRmax, and advise using graded-test data to determine HRmax when available.
limitations: Small convenience sample (n = 99), general population rather than runners; abstract does not give numeric limits of agreement or RMSE; the authors' Fox preference conflicts with the much larger Tanaka and Nes datasets for people older than about 30 and rests on a proportional-bias argument in a small sample.
implications: Do not treat any age-based HRmax as an individual truth: prefer an observed maximum from the athlete's own hard efforts or a field test, and use the equation only as a flagged fallback.
Because of proportional bias, an equation-based HRmax is least reliable for athletes with unusually high or low true maxima; avoid it for setting high-end zones when observed data exist.
